title: Divergent source contributions of PM 10  mass and particulate-bound mercury: insights from an interpretable machine learning framework for air quality management
content: Air quality management is predominantly based on particulate matter (PM) mass concentrations, whereas associated health risks are largely driven by chemical composition, particularly toxic trace metals such as particulate-bound mercury (PBM). However, it remains unclear whether the same emission sources and atmospheric processes govern PM mass and metal-associated toxicity. In this study, an integrated Positive Matrix Factorization – Random Forest – SHapley Additive exPlanations – Partial Dependence Plot (PMF-RF-SHAP/PDP) framework was applied to PM10 and PBM10 observations in Ho Chi Minh City to quantify source contributions, nonlinear relationships, and pollution-dependent variability. Both PM10 and PBM10 exhibited substantial variability, with mean concentrations of 78.1 ± 47.7 µg m−3 and 67.7 ± 46.9 pg m−3, respectively. A total of 183 quality-controlled paired PM10 and PBM10 observations, including 37 independent test observations per target variable, collected during dry and rainy seasons in 2018 were used for model development. The RF model achieved strong predictive performance (R2 = 0.922 for PM10 and 0.603 for PBM10), indicating robust representation of complex interactions among predictors. Source-resolved attribution revealed distinct patterns. For PBM10, anthropogenic factors accounted for 48% of the overall SHAP contribution share, with industrial-related factors representing 65% of the anthropogenic contribution and traffic-related factors accounting for the remaining 35%. For PM10, anthropogenic factors also accounted for 48% of the overall SHAP contribution share, with traffic-related factors representing 59% of the anthropogenic contribution. Atmospheric transport and meteorological factors each contributed 23% of the overall SHAP share. Under high-pollution conditions, anthropogenic emissions became increasingly important for both PBM10 and PM10, although regional transport continued to contribute substantially to the variability of both pollutants. These findings demonstrate that PM10 mass and PBM10 are associated with distinct source-related and environmental patterns, highlighting the need for composition-informed air quality management beyond bulk particulate mass control.
